body.heading: A mathematician in a poet's family
paragraphs: Ada Lovelace was born in 1815, the daughter of the poet Lord Byron, whom she never really knew. Her mother encouraged mathematics instead of poetry, and Ada turned out to be gifted at it, studying with some of the leading mathematicians of the day.

She became fascinated by the work of Charles Babbage, who designed a mechanical computer called the Analytical Engine. It was never fully built, but on paper it had the essential parts of a modern computer: memory, a processor, and instructions on punched cards.

body.heading: Notes that became a program
paragraphs: In 1843, Lovelace translated an article about the Analytical Engine from French and added her own extensive notes — labelled A to G — which ended up far longer than the article itself. In those notes she set out a step-by-step method for the machine to calculate a sequence of numbers called Bernoulli numbers.

That method is widely regarded as the first computer program: instructions written for a machine, published decades before any electronic computer existed. She wrote it for hardware that had never run a single calculation.

body.heading: Seeing further than the machine's inventor
paragraphs: Lovelace also saw possibilities Babbage had not emphasised. She wrote that if the relationships between musical notes could be expressed in numbers, the engine might one day compose music — an early glimpse of computers as creative tools, not just calculators.
She died young, in 1852, and her notes were largely overlooked for a century. Today a programming language, Ada, carries her name, and her story is a reminder that imagination is a technical skill.

takeaway: Ada Lovelace published the first computer program in 1843 for a machine that was never built — and foresaw computers composing music long before they existed.
